propositions.text: Mr. Verhagen applies for judicial review of the Board's decision rejecting his extension of time application.
propositions.quote: The applicant, Mr. Verhagen, applies for judicial review of a decision of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations and Employment Board (Verhagen v. Canada Revenue Agency, 2025 FPSLREB 100) (the Decision). The Board rejected his application for an extension of time to remedy the untimely transmittal of his grievance.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Verhagen applies for judicial review of the Board's decision rejecting his extension of time application.

propositions.text: In December 2021, Mr. Verhagen filed a grievance alleging disciplinary action, constructive dismissal, and Charter rights violation under the employer's COVID-19 vaccination policy.
propositions.quote: In December 2021, Mr. Verhagen filed a grievance against his employer, the Canada Revenue Agency, alleging that its COVID-19 vaccination policy involved disciplinary action, constituted constructive dismissal, and violated his rights under section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, Part I of the Constitution Act, 1982, being Schedule B to the Canada Act 1982 (U.K.), 1982, c. 11.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Verhagen filed a grievance alleging disciplinary action, constructive dismissal, and Charter rights violation under the employer's COVID-19 vaccination policy.

propositions.text: After first-level denial, Mr. Verhagen referred the grievance directly to the Board, claiming the collective agreement allowed this due to constructive dismissal allegation.
propositions.quote: When his employer denied the grievance at the first level, Mr. Verhagen referred it directly to the Board for adjudication. He submitted that the applicable collective agreement allowed a direct referral because his grievance alleged he had been constructively dismissed under the policy.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Verhagen referred the grievance directly to the Board after first-level denial, claiming collective agreement allowed this for constructive dismissal.

propositions.text: The employer argued the collective agreement required grievance presentation at each level, so the Board lacked jurisdiction due to Mr. Verhagen's failure to do so.
propositions.quote: His employer objected to this referral. It argued that the collective agreement required Mr. Verhagen to present the grievance at each level of the grievance process and, because he had not done so, that the Board was without jurisdiction to adjudicate it.

paragraphs.summary: The employer argues the collective agreement required grievance presentation at each level, so the Board lacked jurisdiction due to Mr. Verhagen's failure.

propositions.text: The Board allowed the employer's objection, found grievance not properly before it, and denied referral to adjudication.
propositions.quote: On March 6, 2024, the Board allowed the employer’s objection, concluded that the grievance was not properly before it and denied the referral to adjudication (the First Decision).

propositions.text: The collective agreement and statute require grievances to follow grievance procedure levels; skipping levels requires mutual consent.
propositions.quote: It held that the collective agreement and the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act, S.C. 2003, c. 22, s. 2, required grievances to follow the required levels of the grievance procedure and that parties could skip levels only on mutual consent.

propositions.text: The Board decided collective agreement does not allow grievors to treat first-level reply as final and directly refer grievance based on constructive dismissal claim alone.
propositions.quote: it decided that the collective agreement did not entitle grievors, based solely on their own characterization of their grievance as involving a constructive dismissal, to treat their employer’s first-level reply as a final-level decision and directly refer their grievance to the Board for adjudication.

paragraphs.summary: The Board allowed employer's objection, found grievance improperly before it, and ruled collective agreement requires following grievance levels unless mutually agreed.

propositions.text: After declining judicial review of First Decision, Mr. Verhagen requested grievance transmission to third level, which employer denied as untimely.
propositions.quote: On April 8, 2024, having decided not to judicially review the First Decision, Mr. Verhagen requested his grievance be transmitted to the third level. His employer denied the grievance as untimely, because over two years had passed since the first-level grievance reply, well beyond the 10-day timeframe prescribed by the collective agreement.

propositions.text: Employer denied grievance at final level; Mr. Verhagen referred grievance to Board for adjudication.
propositions.quote: It similarly denied the grievance at the final level. Mr. Verhagen referred the grievance to the Board for adjudication.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Verhagen requested grievance transmission to third level after First Decision, employer denied as untimely, and grievance was denied at final level.

propositions.text: The employer objected to the referral to adjudication based on Mr. Verhagen's untimely grievance transmittal among other grounds.
propositions.quote: The employer objected to this referral to adjudication based on, among other grounds, Mr. Verhagen’s untimely transmittal of the grievance to the third level.

paragraphs.summary: The employer objects to the referral to adjudication based on Mr. Verhagen's untimely grievance transmittal.

propositions.text: Mr. Verhagen argued grievance was timely or alternatively requested extension of time in interest of fairness.
propositions.quote: Mr. Verhagen argued that the grievance had been transmitted in a timely manner. In the alternative, he asked the Board to extend the time to present his grievance “in the interest of fairness” (Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Regulations, SOR/2005-79, para. 61(b)).

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Verhagen argues grievance was timely or requests extension of time in interest of fairness.

propositions.text: Board considered several factors for extension of time, emphasizing clear, cogent and compelling reasons for delay.
propositions.quote: In deciding whether to extend time, the Board considered several factors (Schenkman v. Treasury Board (Public Works and Government Services Canada), 2004 PSSRB 1) but placed considerable weight on whether there were clear, cogent and compelling reasons for the delay.

paragraphs.summary: The Board considered factors for extension of time, emphasizing clear, cogent and compelling reasons for delay.

propositions.text: Time limits for grievance filing are brief and precise to ensure timely dispute resolution and should be set aside only in extraordinary circumstances with clear, cogent and compelling reasons.
propositions.quote: The Board held that the time limits to file a grievance and refer it to adjudication are brief and precise to ensure the timely, simple and expeditious resolution of disputes. It noted that they had been bargained for by the parties and the employer should rightly be entitled to rely on them. It held that they should be set aside only in extraordinary circumstances, established by clear, cogent and compelling reasons that demonstrate that extending time is in the interest of fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The Board held grievance time limits are brief and precise, set aside only in extraordinary circumstances with clear, cogent and compelling reasons.

propositions.text: Board found Mr. Verhagen's novel but unsuccessful legal strategy did not constitute a cogent reason for delay.
propositions.quote: The Board found that by insisting on directly transmitting his grievance to adjudication after the first-level denial, Mr. Verhagen had pursued a novel but ultimately unsuccessful legal strategy and that this did not constitute a cogent reason for the delay.

paragraphs.summary: The Board found Mr. Verhagen's novel but unsuccessful legal strategy did not justify delay.

propositions.text: Board held Mr. Verhagen failed to provide cogent explanation for 23 business days delay to transmit grievance to third level, rejecting his claim about timing of 10-day period.
propositions.quote: Even considering only the time taken by Mr. Verhagen to transmit his grievance to the third level after receiving the First Decision, the Board held that he had not provided a cogent explanation for taking 23 business days to do so—over the 10-business-day time limit for presenting a grievance at each succeeding level. It rejected his claim that the 10-business-day period did not begin to run until the deadline to judicially review the First Decision had expired.

paragraphs.summary: The Board held Mr. Verhagen failed to explain 23 business days delay and rejected his claim about timing of 10-day period.

propositions.text: The Court must review the Decision on the reasonableness standard; Mr. Verhagen must identify significant flaws to render it unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The parties agree that the Court must review the Decision on the reasonableness standard. Mr. Verhagen must identify shortcomings or flaws in the Decision that are sufficiently central or significant to render it unreasonable (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, [2019] 4 S.C.R. 653 at para. 100 [Vavilov]).

paragraphs.summary: The court states it must review the Decision on reasonableness standard; Mr. Verhagen must identify significant flaws.

propositions.text: Mr. Verhagen has not met burden; the Decision is reasonable with rational, logical reasoning considering parties' arguments and legal constraints.
propositions.quote: In our view, Mr. Verhagen has not met this burden. The Decision bears all the hallmarks of reasonableness: in rational and logical reasoning that considers the arguments of the parties, the Board justifies the Decision in relation to the legal and factual constraints that bear on it.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Mr. Verhagen has not met burden; the Decision is reasonable with rational, logical reasoning.

propositions.text: Mr. Verhagen argues Board erred in First Decision finding he did not follow grievance procedure and that constructive dismissal allowed direct referral.
propositions.quote: Mr. Verhagen reiterates that, in the First Decision, the Board erred in finding that he had not followed the grievance procedure. As he did before the Board, he claims that because his grievance alleged constructive dismissal, he could refer it directly to adjudication under the collective agreement.

propositions.text: Because Mr. Verhagen did not judicially review or request reconsideration of First Decision, Board reasonably treated it as conclusive that grievance procedure was not followed and extension of time was needed.
propositions.quote: However, because Mr. Verhagen did not judicially review the First Decision or formally request its reconsideration, it was not unreasonable for the Board to decide that the First Decision conclusively determined he had not followed the grievance procedure and, as a result, that he needed an extension of time to transmit the grievance to the third level.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Verhagen argues Board erred in First Decision; court finds Board reasonably treated First Decision as conclusive due to no review or reconsideration.

propositions.text: Extension of time in interest of fairness is discretionary and factually based; Board did not misapprehend evidence or unreasonably depart from precedent.
propositions.quote: Whether to grant an extension of time in the interest of fairness is a highly discretionary and factually suffused decision. Mr. Verhagen has not shown that in exercising its discretion, the Board fundamentally misapprehended or failed to account for the evidence before it (Vavilov at para. 126). Nor was it unreasonable for the Board to depart from previous authorities, so long as it justified this departure (Vavilov at para. 131). It was entitled to find that the cases on which Mr. Verhagen relied did not afford proper weight to the importance of upholding deadlines to which the collective agreement parties had agreed.

paragraphs.summary: The court states extension of time is discretionary; Board did not misapprehend evidence or unreasonably depart from precedent.

propositions.text: Mr. Verhagen insists he was constructively dismissed and grievance should be heard on merits.
propositions.quote: Mr. Verhagen reiterated at the hearing before the Court that he is certain that he was constructively dismissed and that his grievance should be heard on the merits.

propositions.text: Unless Board's decision is unreasonable, court cannot intervene.
propositions.quote: However, unless the Board’s decision is shown to be unreasonable, we cannot intervene.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Verhagen insists on constructive dismissal and merits hearing; court says it cannot intervene unless Board's decision is unreasonable.

propositions.text: The court thanks Mr. Verhagen for his skill and eloquence in submissions.
propositions.quote: We thank Mr. Verhagen for the skill, organizational ability and eloquence he displayed in making his submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The court thanks Mr. Verhagen for his skill and eloquence in submissions.

propositions.text: The respondent agrees there should be no costs.
propositions.quote: The respondent agrees that there should be no costs.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent agrees there should be no costs.

propositions.text: The court will dismiss the application without costs.
propositions.quote: Therefore, we will dismiss the application without costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court will dismiss the application without costs.
